pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — classify ocean animals into major groups: fish (gills, scales), marine mammals (breathe air, warm-blooded, feed milk), and invertebrates (no backbone — jellyfish, octopus, crab, starfish).
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things' — marine animals are the exemplar set here.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4 / grouping-by-observable-features reasoning; groups defined by shared traits, not habitat.
• Operational details: build on the 5–7 whale/dolphin work — now add INVERTEBRATE (no backbone) as a third group and formalise defining features. Teach a two-question classification key: (1) does it have a backbone? → if no, invertebrate; if yes, (2) gills+scales (fish) or breathes air+milk+warm-blooded (mammal). The backbone/no-backbone split is the big new idea and the main error source (children assume all animals have bones). Use varied, deliberately tricky exemplars (jellyfish, octopus, seahorse-which-IS-a-fish, dolphin, shark).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~7–8): sorts clear cases into the three groups; Tier B (transitional, ~8–9): states a defining feature for each group and uses a simple key; Tier C (~9): classifies tricky cases (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin) by reasoning from features and justifies with the backbone test.
bestPractices: Teach classification as APPLYING A KEY (yes/no questions on observable features), not memorising which animal is in which box — keys are the Y4 curriculum skill and make reasoning transferable.
Foreground the backbone test as the first split: invertebrate vs vertebrate — most ocean animals are invertebrates, which surprises children and corrects 'all animals have bones'.
Use side-by-side defining-feature contrasts (gills vs lungs, scales vs smooth, backbone vs none) with real specimens/photos.
Deploy deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse) so students confront that appearance and habitat don't decide the group — features do.
Have students BUILD/justify a classification, explaining the feature that placed each animal, not just the final bin.
keyRepresentations: A branching classification key (backbone? → gills or lungs?) the child follows
A three-column feature chart: FISH (gills, scales, eggs) / MAMMAL (lungs, warm-blooded, milk) / INVERTEBRATE (no backbone)
A Venn/sorting surface with tricky exemplars to place
Real-photo specimen cards with tappable feature evidence
commonMisconceptions: 'All animals have a backbone / bones' — so children miss that octopus, jellyfish, crab and starfish are invertebrates.
'It lives in the sea, so it's a fish' — habitat, not features, drives the (wrong) grouping (carried over from earlier).
'A whale is a fish because it's big and swims' / 'a dolphin is a fish because it has fins' — classifying by size or body shape.
'A jellyfish/starfish is a fish because the name says fish' — misled by naming.
'A shark is a mammal because it's smart/large' — over-extending the mammal category; sharks are fish (gills, no milk, cold-blooded).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners classify ocean animals into fish (gills, scales), marine mammals (breathe air, warm-blooded, feed milk) and invertebrates (no backbone — jellyfish, octopus, crab, starfish) by running a simple yes/no classification key on observable features rather than memorising which animal goes in which box. The central new idea is the backbone test: most ocean animals are invertebrates, which corrects the assumption that all animals have bones. Deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse) force learners to classify by features, not by habitat, size, name or appearance.

activities.title: Run the two-question key on a mixed tank of sea creatures
feedback: If an octopus is placed with the fish, prompt: 'Check its backbone — does it have one?' to redirect it into invertebrates.
Reward answers that name the deciding feature ('gills', 'no backbone', 'breathes air and feeds milk') rather than just the final group.
When a shark is called a mammal because it is big or smart, show it breathes through gills and has scales and a backbone, so it stays a fish however large.

If the seahorse is set aside because it does not look like a typical fish or because its name has no 'fish', run the key on it: it has a backbone and breathes with gills, so it is a fish despite its unusual shape and name — note its body is covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales, so feature (backbone and gills), not shape or name, decides.
If a learner routes every animal the same way, have them re-run question 1 (backbone?) separately for each animal so one shared trait (lives in the sea) stops driving the whole sort.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is the ACT of classifying by running a key, so learners should perform the key and get immediate feature-based feedback on each animal, including tricky cases that block the habitat/appearance/name shortcut. An interactive sorter that routes each animal from the features selected (tap yes/no on backbone, then gills vs lungs; the animal slides into its group) makes the mechanism live; a physical specimen tray with feature tags works similarly. This proposes the activity; it does not establish that one medium is uniquely effective.
sourceClaims: UK Lower KS2 Y4 science requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways and to explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things.

Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Face a tray or set of cards of mixed sea creatures (fish, dolphin, octopus, jellyfish, crab, starfish, shark, seahorse).
For each animal, answer question 1 first: 'Does it have a backbone?' If no, it is an invertebrate.
If yes, answer question 2: 'Breathes with gills (fish, usually covered in scales) or breathes air with lungs, warm-blooded, feeds milk (mammal)?'
Place the animal in fish, mammal or invertebrate, and say aloud which feature put it there.
Work through the whole tray and notice how many animals (jellyfish, crab, starfish, octopus) end up as invertebrates.
Deliberately try the octopus expecting 'fish', then let the backbone question redirect it to invertebrate.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is the act of applying a key of yes/no questions about observable features; the first split is backbone vs no backbone, and most kinds of ocean animals are boneless invertebrates (in this tray, four of the eight animals are).

activities.title: Build and defend a three-column feature chart
feedback: If a dolphin is called a fish because it has fins, point out fins are not the test: a dolphin breathes air and feeds milk, so it is a mammal.
If a jellyfish or starfish is called a fish because its name contains 'fish', separate the name from the feature: check the backbone instead.
Prompt learners to state a feature for every placement, not just the correct bin.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or paper comparison chart with feature call-outs presents the defining criteria clearly and gives a reference; a scene where tapping an animal reveals its group plus evidence ('invertebrate — no backbone') makes the criteria concrete. This presents and organises the criteria; it does not by itself require the learner to run the key, so it pairs well after the sorter where learners perform the key themselves.
sourceClaims: Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Fill a three-column chart: FISH (gills, scales, typically lay eggs) / MAMMAL (lungs, warm-blooded, milk) / INVERTEBRATE (no backbone).
Set defining features side by side as contrasts: gills vs lungs, scales (most fish) vs skin with hair or fur (mammals, though dolphins have very little), backbone vs none.
For each animal, point to the exact feature evidence that places it, using real photos or specimens where possible.
Explain in your own words why a dolphin with fins is a mammal and a shark is a fish.
activities.intendedInsight: Each group is defined by shared traits you can observe and contrast, and naming the defining feature is what justifies a classification.

activities.title: Stump-the-classifier reasoning talk
feedback: When the reason is 'it swims' or 'it has fins', redirect to the breathing (gills vs lungs) or backbone test.
Accept answers that cite a specific feature; press for the feature whenever only a group name is given.
activities.rationale: Spoken Socratic probing can surface the criterion a learner is using and confront reasoning errors in the moment. It serves as a probe and discussion complement; the broader, repeated classification practice is better carried by the sorting activity. Its efficacy here is proposed, not tested.
learnerActions: Take Socratic questions one animal at a time: 'You tell me — does an octopus have a backbone?'
Justify each answer by naming the feature behind it, not the final group alone.

Answer discriminating probes: 'Two animals both live in the sea and both swim — can they still be in different groups? How?' and 'What one feature would you check first to tell a marine mammal from a fish?'
Explain why a shark is a fish and a dolphin is a mammal even though both are large sea swimmers.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who reasons from features can defend each placement and resist habitat, size, name and appearance shortcuts.

activities.title: Check and apply: sort and defend with a new animal
feedback: Correct answers: shark = fish (gills, scales, backbone); dolphin = marine mammal (breathes air with lungs, warm-blooded, feeds milk); jellyfish = invertebrate (no backbone at all).
If all three go into 'fish' justified by living in the sea, re-apply the feature gate: air or gills? backbone or none?

A strong response sorts all three correctly and applies the same criteria to a new animal such as an octopus; a partial response sorts most correctly but applies features unevenly (e.g. places shark and dolphin but cannot place the jellyfish, or names the group without the feature).
activities.rationale: A categorisation task plus feature questions and a tricky-case item is a direct check of every evidence goal: sort into the three groups, give defining features (gills vs lungs, backbone vs none), and classify at least two animals per group. The two-tier 'what feature?' question forces the criterion into the open, so a learner sorting by habitat or looks cannot reliably produce the correct sort. A recognition check confirms the group but does not by itself elicit a constructed, defended reason, so it is paired with the sort-and-explain task.
sourceClaims: Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Sort at least two animals per group into fish, marine mammals and invertebrates (e.g. shark and seahorse; dolphin and whale or seal; jellyfish and crab), and for each give the defining feature.
Answer a feature question such as 'Which feature makes it a mammal?' (breathes air / warm-blooded / feeds milk).
Classify a new or tricky case (octopus, shark) and state the reason.
Complete the diagnostic: sort a shark, a dolphin and a jellyfish and explain HOW you decided each — which is a fish, which a marine mammal, which an invertebrate, and what feature places each one.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct classification shows up as the right group AND the stated defining feature, especially for a new animal not practised before.

constraints: Groups are defined by shared traits (features), not by habitat; two animals can both live in and swim in the sea yet belong to different groups.
The backbone (invertebrate vs vertebrate) split is the main new idea and the main error source: children assume all animals have bones, so foreground it as the first question.
Teach keys as a transferable skill (yes/no questions on observable features), not as memorising which animal is in which box.

Keep deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse-which-is-a-fish) so appearance, size and name cannot decide the group; resolve each introduced exemplar in feedback rather than leaving it unaddressed.
The seahorse is a vertebrate fish with a backbone and gills but is covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales; resolve it with the backbone/gills test and do not assert typical scales for it.
A recognition or multiple-choice check confirms the group but does not by itself elicit the learner constructing and defending a feature-based reason; pair it with a sort-and-explain task.
A presented chart or tap-to-reveal scene shows the criteria but does not require the learner to run the key themselves; use it as reference alongside active sorting.
This builds on earlier (ages 5–7) whale/dolphin work; invertebrate is the newly added third group.
Egg-laying is a typical fish feature but not universal; do not use it as a decisive distractor, since some fish bear live young and some mammals lay eggs (not among the ocean exemplars here).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and are marked verified:false in the source row.
Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no claim of tested effectiveness is made.

The source row claimed a 2D interactive 'makes that live' and 'cements transfer' and that 3D 'adds nothing'/'poor fit'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite presents the interactive sorter as one concrete way to perform the key and omits the universal superiority/necessity framing.

The source states seahorses and sharks are fish and jellyfish/octopus/crab/starfish are invertebrates; these are consistent with standard biology. Note that seahorses, while fish, are covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales, so the corrected feedback relies on backbone and gills.
Egg-laying is listed in the source's fish feature chart; kept as a typical, not absolute, feature and excluded from decisive learner questions.
'Warm-blooded'/'cold-blooded' is used at an age-appropriate level; it simplifies thermoregulation but is acceptable for ages 7–9.

probeDeeper: 'You called the shark a fish. Which exact feature proves it — and why isn't the dolphin in the same group?'
'An octopus — fish, mammal, or invertebrate? What's your reason?' (new invertebrate case)
'Two animals both live in the sea and both swim. Can they still be different groups? How?'
'What one feature would you check first to tell a marine mammal from a fish?'
assess.correctAnswer: Shark = fish (breathes through gills, has scales, has a backbone). Dolphin = marine mammal (breathes air with lungs at the surface, warm-blooded, feeds its babies milk). Jellyfish = invertebrate (has NO backbone at all). You decide by defining features — gills vs lungs, backbone vs no backbone — not by the fact that all three live in the sea.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by habitat — 'they all live in the sea, so they're all fish'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make features the gate: does it breathe air or use gills? does it have a backbone? Apply to each animal in turn so the sea-dwelling fact stops driving the sort.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're all fish, because they all live in the sea
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts all three in 'fish'; justifies by living in water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a jellyfish (or octopus, starfish) is a fish because it lives in water and moves — doesn't recognise 'invertebrate'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce backbone as the test: feel your own spine, then note a jellyfish has none — it's an invertebrate. Sort a few no-backbone animals (crab, octopus, starfish) into that group.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the jellyfish a fish; can't accept an animal with no backbone

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by appearance — 'it has fins, so it's a fish' — so the dolphin gets miscalled a fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out fins aren't the test: a dolphin has fins but breathes air and feeds milk → mammal. Use the breathing and milk features, not the silhouette.
errorPatterns.distractor: A dolphin is a fish because it has fins
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: reason is 'it has fins/it swims', not gills/lungs or backbone

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by habitat or looks — calls all three fish, or the dolphin/jellyfish a fish; no feature-based reason.
responseLevels.full: Sorts all three correctly (fish/mammal/invertebrate) using defining features — gills vs lungs, backbone vs none — and applies the criteria to a new animal (e.g. octopus), showing classification by feature rather than by where it lives or what it looks like.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts most correctly and names a feature or two, but applies them unevenly — e.g. gets shark and dolphin right yet can't place the jellyfish, or gives the group without the defining feature.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sort these three sea animals into groups and tell me HOW you decided each one: a shark, a dolphin, and a jellyfish. Which is a fish, which is a marine mammal, and which is an invertebrate — and what feature puts each where it belongs?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can classify uses body features (gills/lungs, backbone/none) and gets all three right. A child who classifies by habitat calls them all fish because they live in water; a child who classifies by looks calls the dolphin a fish (it has fins) or the jellyfish a fish (it swims). The second tier ('what feature?') forces the criterion into the open — the correct sort depends on features, so a feature-free sorter can't reliably produce it.
